The Assemblies of God's 1980 position paper explicitly rejects this reasoning: "To hold that all suffering results from negative confessions and indicates a lack of faith contradicts the Scripture. Some heroes of faith suffered greatly, some even died through faith, and they were commended for it."

fields.citation: General Presbytery of the Assemblies of God, "The Believer and Positive Confession" (position paper, approved 19 August 1980)
fields.note: The statement says: "This puts man in the position of using God rather than man surrendering himself to be used of God," and concludes: "To hold that all suffering results from negative confessions and indicates a lack of faith contradicts the Scripture." It also warns the teaching "can often be more detrimental than views which reject Scripture altogether."

fields.citation: Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa Chapter, "A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel" (16 January 2010)
fields.note: The statement concludes: "it is our overall view that the teachings of those who most vigorously promote the 'prosperity gospel' are false and gravely distorting of the Bible ... it can be soberly described as a false gospel," and names it "incompatible with evangelical biblical Christianity." It also rejects "the unbiblical notion that spiritual welfare can be measured in terms of material welfare, or that wealth is always a sign of God's blessing ... or that poverty or illness or early death, is always a sign of God's curse."

fields.citation: General Presbytery of the Assemblies of God, "The Believer and Positive Confession" (approved 19 August 1980); Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa Chapter, "A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel" (16 January 2010)
fields.note: This is the one doctrine in the corpus where the divided tradition is the reader's own. The Assemblies of God's General Presbytery formally rejected positive-confession teaching in 1980 ("To hold that all suffering results from negative confessions and indicates a lack of faith contradicts the Scripture"), but a large independent Word of Faith and charismatic constituency, outside any classical Pentecostal denomination's own governance, continues to teach it. Reporting either half alone would be false to what a Pentecostal reader meets in practice.

fields.citation: Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, "The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable" (10 December 2015), §40
fields.note: Verbatim, §40: "In concrete terms this means that the Catholic Church neither conducts nor supports any specific institutional mission work directed towards Jews. ... Christians are nonetheless called to bear witness to their faith in Jesus Christ also to Jews, although they should do so in a humble and sensitive manner, acknowledging that Jews are bearers of God's Word." The document states its own status in its preface: "The text is not a magisterial document or doctrinal teaching of the Catholic Church, but is a reflection prepared by the Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews." Nostra Aetate 4 (1965), the binding conciliar text, does not itself address institutional mission to Jews at all; the specific no-institutional-mission position rests only on this later, explicitly non-magisterial reflection.
